evals.prompt: I need a new Excel workbook for a portfolio risk assessment. Three tasks: exposure metrics, a sensitivity screen, and a constrained optimization. Set it up properly so my team can actually read it.
evals.expected_output: Locks CREATE mode. Declares the House Style palette profile and records it on Documentation. Builds sheets in order: Menu, Documentation, Dashboard, then the three task sheets named after the actual work; adds a shared-inputs sheet because more than one task consumes the same drivers. Applies tab colors as a purpose code (#000000 menu, #E8E8E8 documentation, #7030A0 dashboard, #FFC000 shared inputs, and one blue level per analytical level with same-level tasks sharing a color; support calculations uncolored). Sets gridlines and row/column headings visible, no freeze panes. Applies the skeleton on EVERY sheet: rows 1-2 blank, title on row 3, columns A and B empty, content anchored at column C, blank row 4, first section bar row 5, content from row 7. Puts method markers in a marker column to the RIGHT of each block, never in column A or B. Builds the shared inputs BEFORE any downstream calculation. Builds the Menu LAST, generated from the actual tab order with swatches read from actual tab colors, links as =HYPERLINK("#Sheet!A1","Sheet"). Does NOT invent specific prescribed sheet names beyond menu/documentation/dashboard. Does NOT merge cells - title bars span by formatting a range with text in the leftmost cell only. Runs the definition of done before delivering.

evals.prompt: Here's our model workbook. Can you check whether it follows a sensible standard and fix what's broken?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this as AUDIT first, not RESTYLE - 'check ... and fix' does not authorize writing. States that AUDIT never modifies the file, produces a conformance report, and asks for approval before any fix. Inspects sheet order, tab colors, view settings, merged cells, the row-3/column-C skeleton, menu order vs tab order, swatch fidelity, hyperlink resolution, cell classification per block, palette coherence, number formats and precision, negative-value presentation, formula integrity, charts, and residual WIP fills. Detects the palette profile by sampling known formula cells AND known typed values: formulas mostly gray-filled means Audit Standard; formulas unfilled with blue/yellow typed values means current House Style; formulas unfilled with gray typed values and orange controls means the legacy house palette (a coherent convention, not a defect); both gray-formula and unfilled-formula patterns present means the workbook is MIXED and that is a blocking finding. Classifies every finding blocking / major / minor with sheet, range, why it matters, and the fix. Includes a 'what is already right' section. Ends with a scoped RESTYLE proposal listing the ranges it would touch, then stops. Works inside Excel through the add-in and reads state back to verify findings rather than assuming them.

evals.prompt: In our sheet, gray cells are the formulas and orange cells are the hardcoded inputs. Can you add a new scenario tab that matches?
evals.expected_output: Locks EXTEND mode. Recognizes the described convention as the Audit Standard profile (orange = every hardcoded input, gray = calculation) and KEEPS it rather than converting to the House Style default - a coherent existing profile is preserved, and converting would be a separate RESTYLE needing approval. Notes explicitly that a gray fill reads DIFFERENTLY under the two profiles - calculation under Audit Standard, output (#F2F2F2) under House Style - and that mixing them is worse than having no convention. Inspects the existing workbook first: tab colors, named styles already defined (reuses them, does not create Input2 or Header_new), the anchor column and title row actually used in that file - and matches the file where it deviates from this standard. Places the new sheet at the correct position with the matching level tab color, adds the menu row in the matching position with the swatch read from the actual tab color. Leaves every existing cell untouched; states that changing existing formatting would silently turn EXTEND into RESTYLE. Applies profile-neutral rules: green font on any formula containing an embedded editable constant, green/red control cells for checks.

evals.prompt: Format the results sheet so the important numbers stand out. Just make the whole output area yellow and bold.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on the instruction while still delivering. Explains the prime directive: classify before formatting, never apply one format to a whole range, because formatting is a claim about meaning. Explains that blanket yellow is doubly wrong under this palette: yellow #FFFF00 is the Input fill for assumptions the user tunes, so painting the output area yellow invites readers to type over formulas; and navy is scarce - Result (navy #000080, Arial 10 bold, white font) is for the decision-critical figure only, and a sheet with thirty navy cells communicates nothing. Proposes the correct split instead: ordinary calculated results take Output (#F2F2F2, Aptos Narrow 11 bold #3F3F3F, thin #3F3F3F border), the one decisive figure takes Result (navy #000080, Arial 10 bold white), a chosen option takes Recommended (#E2EFDA, Arial 11 bold #375623), intermediate steps stay unfilled. Asks which figure is the actual answer if it cannot tell. If the user reaffirms the blanket yellow, treats that as their decision, says so, and applies it - but records the deviation in Documentation.

evals.prompt: Our variance column shows negatives in red with parentheses like accounting does, and a dash for zero. Can you make the new columns match the rest of the workbook?
evals.expected_output: States this standard's negative convention: leading minus sign (-6.69), same black or dark-gray font as positives, no red, no parentheses, no dash for zero - zero displays per the row's format. Explains the reason: in a quantitative assessment negatives are ordinary results (a delta, a drawdown, a residual), and red collides with the FAIL state of the check colors, which ARE alarms. Gives the mechanism: a single-section number format ('0.00', not '0.00;[Red]-0.00' and not '0.00;(0.00)') lets Excel render the minus itself; and no conditional formatting solely to recolor negatives. BUT recognizes that the existing workbook uses the accounting convention coherently: in EXTEND mode it matches the file and notes the deviation, rather than silently introducing a second convention. Changing it workbook-wide is a RESTYLE decision that needs approval.

evals.prompt: The dashboard says our headline metric is 4.28 but the task sheet computes 4.31. Which is right?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the root cause as the most damaging defect in this standard: a dashboard value hardcoded rather than linked. Does not guess which number is 'right' - the task sheet is the source, the dashboard is a stale copy, and the copy has no authority. States the rule: every dashboard value links to the cell that computed it; never hardcode a dashboard result that already exists elsewhere. Fix: replace the typed 4.28 with a cross-sheet reference. Classifies this as a BLOCKING finding - the summary contradicts the workbook and any reader of the dashboard alone is misled. Recommends sweeping the rest of the dashboard for other typed values, and adding a check row (delta between dashboard and source, CheckPass/CheckFail with the delta and the location shown, not just the word OK). Does not attempt to verify whether 4.31 itself is arithmetically correct, and says so explicitly - this skill governs presentation, not the math.

evals.prompt: Can you standardize this legacy workbook? Merged title cells everywhere, no tab colors, and someone hid three sheets.
evals.expected_output: Locks RESTYLE and gates it: requires explicit go-ahead, a backup copy (states the path), and a scope decision - targeted fixes by default, not a full restyle, because a full restyle overwrites coherent local formatting. States the preservation contract: formulas, cross-sheet references, named ranges, data validation, charts, comments, existing named styles, deliberate widths, print setup, and locally coherent formatting all survive. Handles the merges correctly: unmerge only after relocating the value to the leftmost cell, then recreate the title bar by formatting the range with text in the leftmost cell only. Does NOT unhide the hidden sheets without asking - something may be hidden for a reason; reports them instead. Applies tab colors as a purpose code with same-level sheets sharing a color. Delivers a change log table (sheet, range, before, after, reason) plus counts, and says explicitly what was left alone and why. Does not rewrite any formula to 'clean it up'.

evals.prompt: Add a chart comparing the twelve candidate allocations on risk and return, and put the assumptions right next to it so people can play with them.
evals.expected_output: Chooses XYScatter - two metrics plotted against each other, not an ordered sequence, so a Line chart would imply an ordering that does not exist. No 3D. Sets an explicit title naming subject and both metrics, axis titles with units on the analytical scatter, blanks plotted as not plotted (never zero), legend hidden if the colors are explained by the title, green for strong results and red for weak, consistently across the workbook. Places the chart to the right of or below its source data, anchored in empty space so it does not obscure cells. On the 'assumptions next to it' request: distinguishes a genuine scenario CONTROL (yellow Input, #FFFF00, Aptos Narrow 11 #3F3F76, thin #7F7F7F border on all sides - looks like a form field) from base data, and warns against scattering editable values across calculation blocks; prefers a link back to the shared inputs, or a clearly-headed control block directly beside the chart. Does not add decorative conditional formatting and does not convert the range to an Excel table.

evals.prompt: I pulled our GL export and the FX rates in with Power Query. They landed as blue striped tables on two tabs in the middle of the workbook. Tidy that up.
evals.expected_output: Moves both query outputs to the END of the workbook, after the task sheets and any support-calculation sheet. Renames them 'Data <n> <short id>' with the slug matching the Power Query query name - e.g. 'Data 1 gl_export', 'Data 2 fx_rates' - keeping them under 31 characters and noting that the space forces quoting in every reference ('Data 1 gl_export'!C7). Sets tab color #BFBFBF and lists them in the menu, because unlike support calculations these carry the workbook's provenance. Sets the load destination to C6 so the sheet keeps the standard skeleton: rows 1-2 blank, title on row 3, columns A and B empty. REPLACES the built-in Power Query table style: table style set to None, banded rows and columns off, total row off, AutoFilter KEPT (the sanctioned filtering case). Applies SectionHeader (#333399, Arial 9 bold white) to the table header row and SourceData blue #BDD7EE uniformly to the body - explains that a uniform fill is correct here because the whole block is genuinely one semantic class (imported data, filled once by the refresh), and that an unfilled cell inside a PQ table would wrongly read as 'calculated here'. Adds a 'PQ: <simple headline>' caption in RowTitle (#333399, Arial 9 bold, yellow #FFFF00) directly ABOVE the table header row, with PQ in the marker column alongside Py/Model/API. Sets column types IN THE QUERY via a Changed Type step rather than formatting landed cells, then applies display formats per column, uniform down each column: real dates, #,##0 counts, 0.00 amounts, percentages stored as FRACTIONS, leading-zero codes as text. Enables 'Preserve cell formatting' and disables 'Adjust column width' in Query Properties, then REFRESHES ONCE to verify the formatting survives. States that everything downstream must REFERENCE the data, never copy it, and that typing inside the loaded range is silently overwritten on the next refresh. Works through the Excel add-in against the live workbook.
